utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-T --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to the Prosecution, to Mr. Seselj, and to everyone assisting us in this case. We're going to have a witness now. I know that the Prosecution asked for private session before we start, but before we do so, I have a number of administrative questions I need to put to Mr. Mundis. Based on the schedule we had, last week we said that since a witness that was scheduled to testify tomorrow and Thursday is not going to testify, we envisioned showing a number of videos. That's why I asked you to prepare a list of possible videos, to send the list to Mr. Seselj for him to tell us whether he agrees or not, but the Chamber received absolutely no response with regard to this issue, so I don't know where we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Your Honours, the list of videos to be shown was only finalised earlier this afternoon, and I believe it's now been circulated. Perhaps it's been sent to the legal officer. And that document is also, as I speak, being translated into Serbian for the benefit of Dr. Seselj. It did take us a little bit longer to narrow down the list and put it in a format that made most sense from a logical point of view, but I apologise for the late disclosure of that but it has now been done. My case manager has earlier this afternoon circulated that list, and as I say it's being urgently translated into Serbian for the benefit of Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Will Mr. Seselj be able to receive the translation during the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is my understanding, Mr. President, Your Honours, that it is, as I indicated, being urgently translated, and I believe the internal deadline was 6.00 p.m. today. So assuming that we get that via e-mail here in the courtroom it will be immediately printed out and provided to Dr. Seselj prior to the commencement -- or prior to the adjournment for today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Very well. Second question: There was a witness who was supposed to testify on Wednesday and on Thursday. I'm not going to say his name. I don't know if any protective measures had been envisioned for him. But why, why is this witness not coming, because he was supposed to be testifying. Why he isn't he coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I need, Mr. President, to just pull up the schedule that had been circulated that has the information concerning that witness. Do you recall which -- the date on the schedule that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the schedule this -- the witness was supposed to come and testify tomorrow and Thursday. VS-45. That's Witness VS-45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- perhaps while my colleague is addressing the Chamber if there's any other matters I can make -- provide you with the specific information concerning that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last issue I want to deal with. Next week we are supposed to have the expert witness Mr. Strinovic, a forensic expert, someone who conducted post-mortem examinations and so on and so forth. But we realised, I realised, that the Chamber has not received any expert reports. We have not received this expert's report. The only thing I know is that this expert witness has already testified in two cases, and it is my understanding that you want to tender into evidence as an expert report a report that this expert had drafted for a previous case plus the transcript of his testimony in the second case. Can you shed some light on this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, thank you for the opportunity. I know that a large amount of information was conveyed to the Chamber's legal officer and Dr. Seselj, I believe, last week concerning that witness. Due to primarily the witness's schedule, he will not be appearing next week as we had previously indicated or hoped that he would be able to do. So at this point, Your Honours, we're still trying to finalise the schedule for next week, but I will indicate that Professor Strinovic will not be testifying next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. He will not testify next week. Who will be testifying in his place? Have you scheduled other witnesses for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have at this point in time just come from a meeting, excuse me, with VWS and it's my understanding that they have been in a position to schedule Witness VS-33 for Thursday, the 27th, who would likely carry over into the first part of Tuesday, the 1st of April. We are unable at this point to identify any witnesses for the 25th and 26th of March. I am working on that as we speak and hopefully by the end of today, if not the beginning of tomorrow, we should be in a position to have further information concerning the 25th and 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With respect to Professor Strinovic, when do you envision him testifying? At what point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would anticipate at this point, Your Honours, that his testimony would be somewhere in the region or vicinity of the week of the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I am in a position to provide some information concerning Witness 45. I would ask -- are we -- are we still in private session? I need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But before we do so, I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Seselj, because he asked to take the floor. I suppose he wants to address the issue of witnesses. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Judges, there is a far greater problem here than would appear at first sight and that is to do with the expert Strinovic. His expert report doesn't exist at all. I haven't received it. Now, on several occasions I received a document from the Prosecution under the title of "The Prosecution discloses the expert report of Davor Strinovic," or something like that, that title was used. And then what received was a supplementary document of post-mortems, pathological findings, forensic reports, but no expert report as such. I never received that. Now, over the weekend, as the next witness that is coming up, I haven't got many questions to ask him, so I dealt with the other matter throughout the weekend and looked through all the documents, and there is no expert report by Davor Strinovic, and it would appear that there was no expert report in other trials other, but this heap of papers, what they did in these other trials, they put forward this heap of papers, and the counsel didn't pay attention and that passed by as an expert report. It cannot be an expert report. There was a questionnaire that the Prosecution provided him with for him to state his views on certain issues, and that amounts to some 10 pages, but that is not an expert report either. So what I insist upon is this: That the Prosecution disclose Davor Strinovic's expert report first and then to bring him in here to court as an expert, because I don't know what I can challenge if I don't have the report. If you remember, your colleagues still weren't in this Trial Chamber, I sent you a submission in writing about Davor Strinovic's expert report that was intimated and the first point was that in fact I haven't been provided with the report itself, and nothing's changed since that time. And's not the only problem, we have problems with the next three experts as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. We'll deal with this issue first. Mr. Mundis, Mr. Seselj is quite right. I've discovered that there is indeed a document, a ten-page document, but it can't be seen as an expert report. And the question is the following: Will we receive an expert report? Will the expert report be disclosed in due course to Mr. Seselj since you anticipate to call this witness around the 22nd of April? That's the question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The document, I believe, is approximately 13 or 14 pages long. It was a report that was admitted into evidence in the Milosevic case. That, in fact, is the report of the witness Strinovic. In accordance with information that was provided on the 14th of March, we have asked in light of the fact that that earlier report was produced in 2003 that the Witness Strinovic update that to reflect any new or additional information concerning exhumations that have occurred in the intervening few years. We expect or are hopeful that he will in fact update that report and it will be available in the Serbian and English languages as soon as he has done so. That is another reason why this witness has been postponed so that he can be given an opportunity to revise the earlier report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, what happened in the Milosevic case comes under the jurisdiction of that Trial Chamber. But as far as we are concerned we have this 14-page report, I have it in front of me, and -- yes, let me have a look at it. On the first page we have a summary, a summary related to his CV and his employment. And then we have three pages related to the role of forensic pathologists, the way they are used, also related to medical problems in terms of body identification. All the rest is tables. I can show it to you. Just tables. In other words, the expert report comes down to three pages, three pages. Do you intend to give us exactly the same thing, or will the expert conduct and produce a professional report as can be expected? Because that's the report we have. I'm showing it to you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That -- that, Mr. President, is in fact the report I was just referring to. That is the report that Professor Strinovic has produced and which was -- has been admitted into other proceedings before this Tribunal. As I've indicated, he has been asked to revise that report, and we will take the comments of the Trial Chamber on board in terms of the revisions that we will be directing this expert to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect to the memory of the late Slobodan Milosevic, I nonetheless have to say that Mr. Milosevic, when he -- during the Prosecution case, had very scant knowledge of Anglo Saxon law, that a whole Simplon express train could be passed into evidence and there was -- without him noticing, and there was an abuse there by the Prosecution which was tolerated by the Trial Chamber. That is the expert report was admitted into evidence without it ever having existed. There never was an expert report. Now, with respect to this non-existent expert report by Davor Strinovic, I received post-mortem findings for each corpse, several hundred colour photographs of corpses, and I threw away those colour photographs because I'm interested in that. I'm not going to challenge whether there were corpses or not. But as I say there is no expert report per se, so you can't revise something that doesn't exist in the first place and you can't supplement something. Davor Strinovic can't supplement something that was passed through as an expert report in the Milosevic trial. Either Davor Strinovic has to write a real expert report or he can't appear here in the capacity of an expert witness. That's the crux of the matter. Because then you can't have an expert without an expert report. We had Oberschall with his 120 page exert report; we have Yves Tomic with over 100 pages; we had Theunens, his expert report numbered over 400 pages; and now we come to Davor Strinovic without any expert report at all. So I'm preparing myself to cross-examine him, but for that cross-examination to take place he has to write an expert report to begin with. He has to do that or somebody else. It doesn't matter who. But without an expert report which will be disclosed to me on time, he cannot -- the person cannot appear in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, Mr. Mundis, my fellow Judge quite rightly tells me that according to the rules, this report should be disclosed 30 days in advance. Here again we are faced with a problem. The report should be disclosed 30 days before the expert witness comes to testify for the accused to be able to make any relevant comments. Whilst Mr. Seselj was talking, I was having a look at these tables, and I noticed the following: Three locations are mentioned here, Vukovar, Vocin, and Ovcara. These tables contain statistics, figures for shootings, for example, 212 probable; explosions, 115, but we have nothing else. In his report the expert should examine at length what happened in Vukovar, explain what happened when the exhumations took place. He should explain what conclusions the expert's arrived. He should tell us how many people died of gunshot wounds, but difference need to be made between shooting at close range and shooting that occurred during fightings, and some people also died of natural causes. Apparently 17 people died of natural causes. That's the type of problem we're faced with, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand these issues, Mr. President. As I've indicated, we will take the comments of the Trial Chamber on board in terms of requests to the expert to revise the report, and I guarantee you that 30 days -- if we need the full 30 days or Dr. Seselj needs the full 30 days that the rules entitle him to, then the witness will be scheduled well after the 30-day disclosure of the revised report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, I believe that you wanted to raise other matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Throughout the weekend I spent my time looking at pathologists and specialists in forensic medicine, and a similar problem exists with the other three experts. Ivan Grujic, Osman Kadic, around Zoran Stankovic. They are pathologists, specialists in forensic medicine, which the -- whom the Prosecution intends to call as expert witnesses. Now, none of them have provided an expert report, but as opposed to the situation with Davor Strinovic where there's nothing, these other three men have statements which they gave to the Prosecution as if they were ordinary witnesses, ordinary witness statements. Osman Kadic's is two or three pages long where he describes how he conducted the exhumation and concludes that he doesn't know who killed those people, which is quite all right as far as he's concerned. And Stankovic and Grujic, they were interviewed by the Prosecution. Now, if they're going to appear here in court as experts, they, too, have to submit an expert report and not have the Prosecution hear them as ordinary witnesses and then we just are provided with their statements. Ordinary statements are not expert reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, with respect to Grujic, Kadic, Stankovic, the other experts, apparently we do not have an expert report for them. We only have written statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would need to check that before confirming what Dr. Seselj says. I do note, however, that Rule 94 business (A) makes reference to the full statement and/or report of any expert witness. So I'm not certain standing here now that a report is required. The rule talks about statement and/or report. I will leave that alone for the moment. We can return to the issue of expert witnesses perhaps at a later point this week after we've had a chance to verify exactly what the material is. I simply can't respond to each and every issue raised by Dr. Seselj at any one given point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, with respect to these four people, Strinovic, Grujic, Kadic, and Stankovic, who have apparently conducted post-mortem examinations on people who had been killed without having been able to determine in all cases how these people had died, I understand that the Prosecution wants to call these four witnesses in order to establish how these people died, after an explosion, gunshot, and so on and so forth. I thought that you had said that you do not challenge that people have died. What you challenge, on the other hand, is your responsibility in these killings. Well, if you do not challenge the facts, the fact that these people died, is it then useful for you to start attacking these "witnesses"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, of these four men, four experts, I'm not -- don't intend to attack Dr. Osman Kadic, just one of them. He provided a statement about an exhumation. I think it was in Herzegovina or Ubopak or something like that near that particular locality, I'm not going to have a barrage against him, but the other three have to be prepared for an attack on my part. I'm going to challenge them in the moral and professional sense, and I have a lot of arguments to do that. So if they bring those three men here, they're going to have a whole artillery firing shoot from me. And for Zoran Stankovic, I said several years ago already, I intimated that in the special Defence brief where I presented many things that I know about Zoran Stankovic and his immoral behaviour, his wheeling and dealing, manipulations, and so on and so forth. So of the Serb pathologists they found the worst lot. And so he has to come in here and face the firing squad from me. Had they chosen an honourable man instead of Zoran Stankovic, and he was the former minister of defence, and that former minister of defence is going to come up against a veritable firing squad from me, a barrage of attacks from me. Now, Mr. President, what is the main problem here is that the Prosecution is taking this too extensively. Had certain facts been dovetailed here, I don't challenge that in Ovcara 200 people were killed, and when I cross-examined the witnesses I didn't challenge that. Those victims were prisoners of war. They were killed there. Most of them were executed by firing squad. Some were killed with knives. I don't challenge that there were killings in certain other locations either, but it is up to the Prosecution to present this to the Trial Chamber in the proper way. Why would it inundate the Trial Chamber with enormous amounts of documents referring to each individual autopsy if this could be done in a more rational way? I know that you have to have proof and evidence for the crime base, but it's up to the Prosecution to offer up something which would be rational and relevant in this courtroom and without the need to waste time with cross-examining false witnesses. Now, as far as Ivan Grujic and Davor Strinovic are concerned, they conducted autopsies over Serb victims, too, and I have a lot of professional questions to ask them there. As for Zoran Stankovic that everything he did he did unprofessionally, there too I would have a lot to say. So either the Prosecution is going to bring in some honourable expert witnesses, one would be sufficient to present a report here and then me say that I have no objections to make. I have no reason to challenge the expert witness in the moral sense or the professional sense, or are they going to bring in somebody -- some people who are a challenge to me and throughout the time that I have at my disposal I will be taking up my heavy artillery. So I am in fair of a reasonable solution but not at all costs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no other issue to deal with, but I will move into private session for a few minutes. Mr. Mundis will now explain why Witness 45 will not be testifying, and he'll talk about the following witness as well. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Very well. Good afternoon, sir. Could you please stand up. Can you please tell me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th of January, 1934, Emil Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified in this Tribunal or before another court about the events that occurred in your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took part in the trial in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Do you remember what case it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were Slavko Dokmanovic, Slobodan Milosevic. Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you ever testified in your own country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but not with respect to these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before what court was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the names of the accused in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember any more. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'm now going to ask you to read the solemn declaration that's being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may be seated. Sir, let me explain to you how we're going to proceed. You will have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor. You have met him already. You met him yesterday as part of the proofing session in advance of this hearing. The Prosecutor may show you a number of documents. After that first stage, Mr. Seselj, who is sitting on your left and who is the accused in this case, will also ask you a number of questions as part of what we call here the cross-examination. He will have as long as the Prosecution to do so. One hour and a half for the Prosecution, an hour and a half for Mr. Seselj. At any time the three Judges sitting before you may ask you questions. Please try to be very accurate in your answers. If you do not understand the question, please ask the one putting that question to you to rephrase it. If you can't remember something very clearly, do not hesitate to say that you can't remember. If at any time you need to rest, if you feel tired, if there's anything wrong with you, just raise your hand and tell us about it and we'll adjourn the hearing. It is customary for us to have a break every hour and a half, but if you do not feel well, if you need for us to stop, notify us immediately. And at any time you may ask a question to the Judges. The Judges will answer any question you may put to them. These are just -- just some information I wanted to give you before you testify, but you've already testified here several times, and you know how we proceed. I'm now going to give the floor to the Prosecutor who will begin the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I start, I didn't have any chance to introduce my colleague, Ms. Divya Prasad who is sitting right to me, to you. It is the first time that she appears here in the courtroom. And we are also assisted by our intern, Kevin Grigsby, who is sitting behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber welcomes Ms. Prasad, who is here for the first time, and would also like to greet the intern assisting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, first I want to start with your private and professional background. Could you tell us what is your nationality and what your ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat. That's my nationality. Born in 1934. Fericanci near Nasice. Those are the essential points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I am married, yes, and I have a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you tell us which school you visited after having finished the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: After elementary school I went to the secondary medical school first, and having completed secondary medical school I attended a higher medical school which I graduated from in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when did you start working?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That was a very long time ago. After I completed my secondary school education I started working straight away, and I graduated from the higher medical school while I was working. So I studied and worked at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the name of the city where you started working?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I started working in Zagreb. After Zagreb, when I got married, I went to work in Vukovar. First of all, I was the head of the central medical laboratory for blood transfusion, the department for blood transfusion, and then after that I worked as a sanitary inspector for the Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already told us that you graduated later on. Can you remember the years when you graduated?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That was around 1970. In the 1970s. That's when I graduated. I did well in my exams, and I had the honour of having excellent professors. I was very satisfied with my professors, and they helped me a great deal in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correct that you at the same time worked and studied for having your examination to graduate at university?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked and studied at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I now want to come to the events when the war was starting. Can you remember when the war started in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It started in a very unfortunate time -- at a very unfortunate time, after the Serbian military forces attacked the Croatian military forces, and they were very poor, poorly equipped with respect to weapons. They practically had no weapons, and they had to seize the weapons from the enemy. Vukovar fell, and I was caught up in that. I was in the Vukovar Hospital. I worked there for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cakalic. I asked you if you remember when the war started. Can you give us the year and the month the war started in Vukovar? Can you give us the year and the month?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I think it was -- I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It's okay. Can you tell us if you have been involved in the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us on which side?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: On the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was your task defending Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, as the Croatian army had been established or was being established, some other things had to be done as well, not just to form an army. So as a sanitary inspector I issued an order that food be cooked separately for the Croatian defenders, and that they should be supplied with food at the place where they were at their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was this work different from the peace times, or was it more or less the same work which you did before the war started?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The job I did was similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where did you live during the war?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I lived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you have to change, because of the war events, your apartment?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Not at that time yet. We didn't have to change our apartment yet, but after the fighting stepped up my wife and I left our own apartment, and we went to the Vukovar Hospital and stayed there, which is where I worked as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us which month that was?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That was November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was it dangerous to go from your apartment to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was. There was shooting. We were being shot at. We were quite near the hospital, some 500 metres away from it, and we had to take a roundabout route to avoid drawing attention to us. We were the last Croats to leave our homes, my wife and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you arrive unhurt to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have there been any problems to enter the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I did not have any problems, but my wife did, but we solved her problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you explain why you didn't have any problems?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Because I was an employee in the medical centre of Vukovar, in that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were you known to the other staff of the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Everybody knew me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was that the reason that later on your wife could also enter without any problems at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe to us how was the situation inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The hospital was full of wounded, full of sick people. The surgical ward had a lot of work to do, especially Dr. Njavro, who was one of the principal surgeons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How was the hygienic situation in Vukovar -- in the hospital, sorry.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We did our best to keep the hygiene conditions good. However, it was very difficult to achieve that. There were a lot of people who had been wounded and who had been killed on both sides. And what I can tell you is that the soldiers who were on the opposite side were protected in equal measure just like the Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have only been patients and refugees in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. There were regular patients who were really ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: But only patients and refugees in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were wounded soldiers there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember if later on when you already were in the hospital other people arrived to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The whole courtyard of the Vukovar Hospital was full of people from Vukovar and the surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did soldiers arrive into the hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They did arrive, Croatian soldiers, until the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did also Serb soldiers arrive to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, after the hospital fell. Was captured, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will come back to another thing which I forgot. Where have you been accommodated, you and your wife, in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: By the X-ray department. My colleagues worked in that department, so they took my wife and myself in and many others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When Vukovar fell you told us that Serbian soldiers entered the hospital. Did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a bit difficult. As soon as the Serb soldiers entered all of us who were there, those of us who were in the hospital, were taken out into a part of the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: May I ask --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, may I ask you does the name Marin Vidic say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was his function, and what did happen to him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was in charge of affairs -- he was in charge of protection, anything to do with protection, and to tour the terrain around Vukovar and Borovo. We would do that together. When we went to Borovo, we were shot at. When we were on our way back we were shot at again, but we managed to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did something happen to Marin Vidic inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was transferred from the municipality to the hospital. He had his office there. I cooperated with him. We were on good terms for a long time. Two officers turned up, officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, Mr. Sljvancanin and Mr. Radic I think his name was. They arrested him and took him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: From where did you know Major Sljvancanin?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I saw him on hundreds of photographs, and I knew him. I knew him. I knew his face. He would come frequently to the Vukovar Hospital after it fell, and they would take people off, and I never saw those people again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when Marin Vidic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That was towards the end of November. I can't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When Marin Vidic was arrested, could you and the others, the other refugees, stay inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We did stay in the hospital for some time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you stay there all the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, no, we couldn't stay there the whole time, because Dr. Bosanac, the lady doctor, demanded that all persons who were not employees of the medical centre should not perform their jobs any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has there been a moment when you and the other refugees were asked to leave the hospital and go outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was requested, too, but it couldn't happen because the entire courtyard was full of people, people who were seeking refuge in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who asked you to leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Dr. Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember if you have been asked to go to the courtyard and did you go there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did go to the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who asked you to go there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Dr. Vesna Bosanac received an order from somebody saying that all people not employed in the medical centre should leave the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who ordered Dr. Bosanac to do this?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people were asked to leave the hospital to go to the backyard?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I can't really say how many exactly, but at least 30 or 40 people. Those who were in good health. Those who had been injured, they stayed in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What did you have to do when you arrived at the backyard of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of corpses there of soldiers from both sides, and a selection had to be made and the necessary steps taken so that these dead bodies could be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And the other refugees who were not dead, what did they have to do at the backyard?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They had to leave the yard after the enemy army turned up. The hospital had been taken over by them, so the people had to leave the yard, leave the compound. And a large column was formed, a column of people, and they were taken off towards the court and the town and Vuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What happened to -- sorry. What happened to you and others in the backyard? Have you also been in columns and left the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We left too. We left the courtyard, too, and a selection was undertaken. The Serb soldiers turned up, and they demanded that all those who were not employees of the medical centre should leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Should leave what?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Should leave the medical centre or the backyard of the court of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both. Both these things. Some people stayed on in the hospital, those who were sick or who were thought to be in a difficult state, a serious state. They stayed on for treatment. The others left. And I have to say that there was a Serb soldier there who had been captured, and he was given better care than the Croatian soldiers were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you describe us the circumstances how you had to leave the backyard of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There was a man called Pero there. He was from somewhere in Bosnia. That's how he introduced himself anyway. And he started swearing at us. He was very uncivilised. He used different swear words, and we hated this. I don't like anybody swearing and invoking my parents' names, especially close family members. We found that insulting. And after a certain amount of time we had to leave and board buses. The buses were checked and we were checked, and this was done by Mr. Sljvancanin. Yes, that's right. It was Mr. Sljvancanin who went through all the buses to see who was in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before you entered the buses, how have you been checked?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Everything we had with us had to be checked and set aside, any bags or anything like that, and we had a lot of unpleasantness, particularly -- well, we were called out and called names and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were there only soldiers, Serbian soldiers, who called you these names and who ordered you to show -- to show everything you have and give it to them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They asked us to hand over everything we had. They even looted. They knew what would probably happen to us. And after that they drove us off of to the Vukovar barracks, and at the Vukovar barracks we waited for about four to five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, sorry to interrupt. We come to this later. You didn't completely answer my question. Have there been only soldiers or also other -- let's call them militaries who were in the backyard of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, there was Major Sljvancanin at that time, and there were -- there was this other man. They came to see us. His deputy. I can't remember his surname just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know the expression "volunteers"?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were people who voluntarily went to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Had volunteers also been at the backyard of the hospital or only soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were also volunteers who cursed and who were in fact more dangerous than the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "more dangerous"?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The soldiers probably had some sort of ethics. They were real soldiers. The ones who were not soldiers, they beat people up, although there were soldiers who beat people up also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many buses arrived?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were six buses which were full. We filled the buses. When the buses were full, they remained standing there in front of the hospital for another half an hour or an hour. Then they turned round and drove off through the town as far as the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember in which bus you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I think I was in the third one, but I can't remember precisely. I think I was in the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you select the bus by yourself?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Now tell us -- you already told us that they drove you to the barracks. Can you tell us if you have been guarded inside the buses?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers walking round the buses. There were also persons there who were not soldiers who said, "Give me this Cakalic. Let me kill him. Give me this one. Give me that one," and so on and so forth. People swarmed there. And I don't think this was done properly, because the army that occupied Vukovar should have taken on this obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please explain us, where did this happen, in front of the hospital or in front of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: This was in the barracks. At that time, there was a staff which was holding its session in that barracks, and they were deciding on the fate of us who were in the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you also been threatened and how?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't show themselves to us. They simply made the decision, and those who carried the decision out, they were other people, different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You told us you had to wait in front of the barracks inside the buses and that people who were outside were threatening or making signs to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sljvancanin was even there. He turned up. I saw him, but in the last part. Whether he brought someone there or not, I don't know. I don't know for what reason he arrived there. We never learned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has there been a person inside of your bus who has specifically been threatened?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They threatened all of us. Some people outside the buses, some in the buses. They said, "Give me this one. Let me kill him. Give me that one. Let me kill him." That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember a person who had the nickname Veliki Boljer?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him. I remember him. He was killed in -- at Ovcara, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has this person also been in your bus while you were still waiting in front of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has he been threatened also?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. More than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe us how?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They said they would kill him, and in the end it happened in the hangar at Ovcara. They killed him by kicking him, beating him with fists, beating him --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, sorry to interrupt. We come to this later. We are still in front of the barracks. Do you know a man called Vlado Kosic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. We worked together in the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has he also been there in front of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He and his wife were in front of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did they address you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He passed by the bus I was in, and he said, "Hey, Emil. See what's happened to you." And I said, "Well, I'm not the only one here. There are lots of people who are going through the same thing. But whatever you're doing, it's immoral."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did he say something related to the bus you were sitting in?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He said, "You're sitting in that bus, but you haven't found yourself a good place." I said to him, "Well, what would be a better place?" And he said, "Well, it's all the same. You'll all end up the same anyway." We were already beginning to gain some idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long approximately you were waiting inside the buses in front of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, it went on for about two and a half or three hours, but I omitted to say before, I accidentally omitted to say this, another bus was brought in subsequently to the barracks, but it was at some distance from us, some 200 or 300 metres away, so that we couldn't know who was in the bus, where it was from, until somebody said the people in that bus are also for shooting. I apologise for forgetting to say that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to get back to Mr. Vlado Kosic, whom you knew and who spoke to you about matters which worried you. Vlado Kosic, was this person a member of the JNA, a member of the Territorial Defence, or did this person belong to another unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was wearing a -- an army uniform. I think he had some sort of rank, but I can't recall what rank it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this a JNA uniform, a Territorial Defence uniform, or maybe another one? What do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that it was a military uniform, the cap, the trousers, and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When the buses left from the barracks, in which direction were they going?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We set out from the courtyard to the road towards Negoslavci, but we didn't enter Negoslavci. Instead, we were taken to Jakobovac, and next to this place called Jakobovac soldiers were ready who directed us to the hangars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I want to know, we are still in Vukovar, and you left in the direction of Ovcara, as far as I understood. Please correct me if I am wrong. Did you also pass the Vuka River?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the bridge you were passing?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar could we please have on the monitor 65 ter number 2521, and it's the sixth picture which has the ERN number 00531235.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, do you recognise this picture, and can you describe us on which bridge you were driving?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Across the bridge over the River Vuka. There's more than one bridge over the River Vuka, but this is the central bridge right in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you realise something unusual as you were passing the bridge, or did you observe people there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were soldiers there. There were soldiers there and some other persons, and some other persons too. But our bus, the one we were in, didn't stop there. It went on towards the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to show to the witness the video clip which has the ERN number 65 ter 6039, and I would like to ask the witness if he recognises this scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] No, it wasn't good. "I got used to better collaboration with JNA than what I'm getting today. "He expected better collaboration with the JNA. "And then today, what is this about? What's the problem. "The Colonel knows all the problems. "The Colonel knows what the problems are. "Well, there aren't any problems. There's the Colonel. "The problem is that I can see soldiers walking in the streets. I see trucks going in, passing by over there."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you witness this or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we were passing over the bridge, on the River Vuka. We saw Mr. Sljvancanin and this other gentleman. I can't remember his last name. They were talking. They were having quite a heated conversation, and Mr. Sljvancanin said to him, "This is not your town. This is my town now, our town," meaning belonging to the occupying army, and they had to remove themselves. These persons, the peacemakers, had to go away. Major Sljvancanin was agitated. I would have been agitated in his place too. He had to take appropriate measures, but I don't know whether this man was from Austria or where he was from, the one who was talking to Mr. Sljvancanin, but there was another gentleman there, too, whom I met in the hospital, Mr. Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, from where do you know what they were talking about? You were sitting in a bus.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they were talking about. I saw them talking, but I don't know what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: But you were telling us some moments ago what they were speaking about. You said, "This is not our town," and, "They have to remove themselves."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, because that was said so loudly. Mr. Sljvancanin said it in such a loud and clear voice that it could be heard very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not understand everything, but these sentences you could understand?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly. I couldn't hear everything they were saying, but I did hear this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: If we can please see again the picture which was first shown on the monitor, 65 ter 2521, and I would like to ask the witness to show us where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you see this picture. Could you please show us with this pen where was the location where you observed this.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: What specifically are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where you saw the scene we have seen on the video clip just a moment ago, where you saw Mr. Sljvancanin.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He crossed the bridge, and the conversation between him and the others took place in front of a confectioner's shop on the bank of the River Vuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you able to mark this on this photo?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was like this. Around here. Perhaps a little bit closer to here. There was a patisserie here, and everything that took place was in front of this Njegic's shop. Njegic was the owner of the patisserie, but it was closed just as everything was closed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. For me this is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could I have admitted this picture and the video clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall have two exhibit numbers: One for the photograph and one for the video clip.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the annotated photo will be Exhibit number P283, and the video will be exhibit number P284.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I now come to the events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I would like to ask a question from the witness. We have just seen a video clip in which we see a member of the ICRC talking with the captain or colonel, I can't remember, Sljvancanin. I was listening very carefully to what you were saying. You said that this officer seemed agitated. This is not the feeling I had on looking at the video clip, but were you present? Were you there when this discussion took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a conversation between Mr. Sljvancanin and this other person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't present there. We only saw them and then we crossed the bridge towards the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were not standing next to these two people, but you saw them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did see them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many metres away were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 35 or 40 metres away, but Mr. Sljvancanin was very loud. You could hear him very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There's something I can't understand, but perhaps we will be able to understand better. On listening to this conversation between these two people, one has the feeling that Mr. Sljvancanin is against or does not want to allow the international community members to go where they please, but straight after that we see a convoy. We see the ICRC vehicle that is following the convoy, so I don't quite understand what's happening. This vehicle has ICRC markings on it. Could you tell us how we are supposed to understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see that convoy either, because we had already crossed the bridge over the Vuka, and we were on our way towards the Vukovar barracks. So I didn't see that convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I now want to come to the events in Ovcara. What could -- what happened when you arrived at Ovcara? Could you please describe this to us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The first bus came to a halt, and everybody disembarked and went to the hangar in Ovcara. The same happened with all the buses, the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth. I was in the third bus, and we entered the hangar in front of which was the president of Vukovar municipality also. He was kicking people and punching them. He kicked and punched whoever of the prisoners he could lay hands on. Slavko Dokmanovic. And he said, "Oh, Inspector. Look at our Emil. You're here too." And I said, "Yes, I am. But nobody is here of their own free will. We're all here under pressure of the enemy army, if I may say so."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you left the bus, did you directly go to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: First we had to take off all our things, clothes, money, everything else we had. They robbed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who is "they," and who ordered you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They started doing it of their own accord. These were persons in JNA uniforms, and there were also people who did not have the entire uniform on. Some had only the bottom part of the uniform. Others had only the top part of the uniform on. So I wouldn't say they were real soldiers. I would say they were other lads who had come there to steal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you also been searched?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You told us some time ago that you have already been searched in the Vukovar Hospital before leaving. Did the people still have some wallets with them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They searched me when we got to Velepromet. I wasn't searched in the first place where they were doing this but the third one, and one of them said, "Oh, look, there's good money here, good money."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you lose only your money, or did you lose also something else?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I lost my money. I was beaten up. They pushed us all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, at this stage I must put a question to you. I was listening very carefully to you, and I watched the video clip a moment ago. One has the feeling, please tell me if I'm wrong, from the outset the JNA seems to be controlling the situation, and then according to what you say, we see things happening. We see things -- we see people who come and assist the army and other people, and then there are some people who are going to rob you and steal your money. What I'm interested in this, who are these people? Who are these people that latch on to the soldiers who come and mistreat and rob the prisoners? Could you tell us who these people are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: When we were entering Velepromet these were conscripts. They searched us and everything we had, money and so on, they took and put in their own pockets, and they said about me, "Look at this one. He's got money," and they took money from me. These were conscripts. They didn't beat us. They only robbed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has there been an event with your glasses?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that happened later. That happened at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please let us know what happened to your glasses?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: One of them took them off and put them on his own nose, saw that they weren't the right size, threw them down onto the ground and stepped on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were you still able to see and to observe without glasses?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I could, but barely. Not very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before you entered the hangar, what happened? Could you please describe us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We got off the buses, the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth, in order, one by one, and then we went into the hangar. Beside the hangar there were people wearing military uniforms and also others who were not in military uniforms. When I entered the hangar, as I was going in Slavko Dokmanovic, who was the president of the municipality of Vukovar, otherwise a friend of mine, we socialised, said, "Look who's here, our inspector. Emil, you're here too. What are you doing here?" And I said, "Well, I'm doing the same as the others." And then we entered the hangar. Had that happened to him, I would have pulled him out of the hangar, and I would have pulled many others out if I was in his position. However, Slavko came to realise that he had done something that was amoral, that he did something that was amoral, and disappeared soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, have there been people beaten up before entering the hangar or have they beaten up in the hangar or has nobody been beat up? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They were beaten. Those who stepped off the buses, as well as those who went into the hangar as well as those who were inside the hangar already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where were they beaten before entering the hangar and how did this happen? Please describe this to us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: As they were stepping off the buses they were beaten straight away. As they were moving towards the hangar, they had to take off parts of their clothing and footwear, and they were beaten there too. As they entered the hangar itself they were beaten there, too, at the entrance. Even inside the hangar. They would beat them up inside as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you also been beaten up before the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember if also elderly people have been beaten up, and do you remember -- can you give us names?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, there was Dr. Bosanac. That was -- well, the lady doctor, Dr. Bosanac, was the wife. So this was the husband. He was positioned beside the door, and they beat him. He was an elderly man. I don't know how old he was, but certainly around 80. And when they brought him there to sit down, they just put him there and had him sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was he the husband of Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, the father. Oh, her husband's father. Her father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you entered the hangar you still have been beaten -- have you still been beaten?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They continued with the beatings, and then some new people appeared. For example, Milan Bulic appeared. I testified against him in Belgrade. And some others, too, whose surnames I did not know. But I knew Milan because he used to work in the kitchen of the Vukovar Hospital at one time, and I would go there to inspect. So that was how I was able to identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did beat me. He beat me. He hit me with a metal baton or some sort of baton and broke two of my vertebrae, and I have problems with that today. My vertebrae in the neck. And I find it difficult to lie down and sleep because my neck hurts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're telling us that Milan Bulic beat you up and that you testified against him in Belgrade. That is a very relevant piece of information for us Judges. Did you testify a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About two years ago. And they called me about 15 days ago too. Well, not 15 days. It was probably a month ago. But I wasn't able to respond to the invitation because I didn't like certain matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You testified two years ago in Belgrade against Milan Bulic. To your knowledge, was this man Bulic sentenced or convicted by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was. The court convicted him, but we received some information to the effect that he was actually walking around Belgrade and that he wasn't actually in prison. Now, whether he is or is not, I don't know that, but that was the rumour going round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you remember what was the length of this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think approximately 15 years. I can't tell you exactly what the sentence was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was sentenced to 15 years, but now he's walking around in Belgrade. Things might get clearer later on about this, but apart from this, this Mr. Milan Bulic, was he a member of the JNA, of the Territorial Defence? Was he a member of another unit? Was he a soldier? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He belonged to some other units, but he wore the Chetnik cap, and he came to the hangar twice. The first time was when I was inside that same hangar, and he same the second time when I'd already been saved and when I already left the hangar. But he wore this sort of cockade, a big one like this. That's what I saw him wearing. And he boasted about it. I'm sorry that he behaved in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that he had a cap, a Chetnik cap. What is it? What is a Chetnik first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a unit, a formation, people associated in one particular formation, and these people did many evil things to many people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And according to you, you -- you could tell them apart because of their cap, because of the cap they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by their caps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, please proceed, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, could you tell us if the prisoners inside the hangars were beaten with objects or only with fists and feet?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Metal batons, wooden batons, with their hands and legs. Whatever came to hand that's what they used to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened to Damjan Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a man who was older than me. He was about ten years older than me. And he was brought to the hangar. They threw him on the floor of the hangar. Bulic was there too along with some others whose names I don't know. And they beat him for a very long time until he succumbed and died. When those soldiers moved away from him I jumped up. I went up to this man Damjan. I took his pulse to see if he gave off any signs of life, because I would have been able to save him by resuscitation, because I was a health worker. However, he was already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, he was killed. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was the only one who was killed, or did you observe another killing?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They killed some others, too, but I don't know their first or last names. Obviously these were people I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe us how you were able to leave the hangar.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: A soldier -- let me just try and remember his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: May I assist the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please help me out here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Does the name "Cevo" say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Stevan Zoric. Stevan Zoric. He wore Chetnik clothing and entered the hangar. He saw me and said, "Come on, Emil, come over here," because we knew one another. So I went outside, but I said, "I don't want to because you're going to kill me." And he said, "No, I'm going to save you." And he did save me. He showed me where to stand, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were you in a position to observe what happened inside the hangar when you were pulled out?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Through a door that was slightly ajar. There were a lot of soldiers and Chetniks there already, and they did a lot of beating. I don't know how many young men were killed, but a great deal, many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So you could observe this beating from outside the hangar looking inside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: From time to time the door would open and close, so you could look into the hangar. And the door had slits in it, too, so you could see through the door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us that you witnessed the killing of Samardzic since he was killed under your very eyes. You were an eyewitness to a -- the beatings of other people, and you yourself were beaten up. We know this. You told us about this. But what's relevant for us here is to find out who did this, who are the perpetrators, and you told us that a Chetnik, someone that you knew, Stevan Zoric, saved you. He pulled you out of this hangar. At this stage of your testimony, any reasonable Judge will ask the following question: Who was in charge of the operations against the detainees in the hangar? Who were these people? Can you tell us some more about it? Can you tell us who inside the hangar was doing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you their names because there were a lot of people that we didn't know there, but the soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army then withdrew. They didn't do those things. It wasn't them. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're telling us that the JNA soldiers had withdrawn. In other words, people you do not know were there, people who probably came from somewhere else, and you're telling us that these people were Chetniks. What information can you give us about these Chetniks? Where did they come from? How were they dressed? How did they speak? Did they have a commander? What can you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They came in an organised way. Now, where they came from I don't know. However, I know that they entered the hangar and beat people. That's the truth of it. However, you must understand that the situation was a very difficult one, because everybody looked out for himself so that they would be safe. Those who remained, they were beaten severely. Now, I didn't see this, but allegedly there were others who succumbed and who died as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the interests of justice, I'm going to quote part of the written statement you made in 1995. The Prosecutor is not asking you this question, but I have to ask you that question because of the relevance of these Chetniks. In your written statement, you said that there were Chetniks who were from Montenegro and that they wore traditional caps and that you recognised them because of a dialect they spoke. Were the Chetniks who were inside the hangar, were they the same Chetniks who may have come from Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... this. I have to go back a little to Velepromet. In -- they appeared in Velepromet for the first time, and they swore at us all kinds of swear words which I wouldn't like to repeat. They would say, "We'll do you in." And they came to Ovcara too. Now, I wasn't there any more, because several of us who were saved -- it was dusk already, and we were taken off to a school, a building that used to be a school on the agricultural farm, and it was by this school that we waited. We waited for the soldiers to come by and take us away from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question relates to the Chetniks who were inside the hangar, those who killed Samardzic, those who beat you up, those who beat up other people. Did you hear them speak? Did you -- you probably heard them say something. You told us that they were not locals. According to you, where did these people come from, if you can tell us. If you can't, obviously, tell us you can't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where they were from. Probably they had come from somewhere in Serbia judging by their dialect. Well, we didn't focus our attention on them. We were focusing on the people who were doing the beating, although there were people doing the beating on one side and on the other side and so on. But in my opinion, it was an organised way of having everybody beaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but organised by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably those who did the beating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you have no idea who organised them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why did this Chetnik you knew, this Zoric, why did he come and save your life, for what reason? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he said, "Emil, come out of there. I'm going to save you. You did me a good turn once, and I'll return the favour now." Now, what happened was this. He suddenly disappeared somewhere, and I assumed that I would have to go back to the hangar. However, three officers turned up, JNA officers, who took over. They took matters into their own hands, and now law and order of sorts was restored. They were short men, short build. I don't know what their names were, but we were saved. There were six Croats and one Serb. We were saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling us there were six Croats and one Serb. Was there also a Serb who was detained together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. He was captured and beaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why? How come he was captured by Serbs, him being a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there you are. He happened to be in the column most probably, and he was spared and saved together with us when we left Ovcara. The -- or his mother came, or I don't remember who it was, and then he went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question before I give the floor to the Prosecution. Was Mr. Zoric dressed like the others, like the others who were in the hangar, or was he dressed differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was dressed -- well, he had an army uniform on his upper half, and what he -- his trousers were like, I can't remember whether he had a complete set of a uniform or not, but the upper part was certainly a uniform, and he had a cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he wear a Chetnik cap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
